extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of English law; legal historians; general readers of Blackstone's Commentaries
extracted.subtask_description: Expository legal commentary describing the origins, creation, incidents, and privileges of the peerage, the organization and limits of the military/militia, and the maritime state under English law. Intended as doctrinal background rather than procedural rules for filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of baronies
rubrics_metrics.description: The most probable opinion seems to be, that they were the same with our present lords of manors; to which the name of court baron... gives some countenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that originally lords of manors (court baron) held seats in the great council; cites Magna Carta and the later division into greater barons summoned in person and smaller ones summoned by sheriff, giving rise to separation of the two houses of parliament. Historical enquiry and antiquarian debate acknowledged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of peerage originally territorial
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of peerage seems to have been originally territorial; that is, annexed to lands, honors, castles, manors, and the like, the proprietors and possessors of which were (in right of those estates) allowed to be peers of the realm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: bishops sit in Lords by succession to ancient baronies annexed to episcopal lands; possession of castle of Arundel adjudged to confer an earldom. Later alienations made dignity personal rather than tied to tenure; record of writ of summons admitted as sufficient evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of creation of peers (by writ or patent)
rubrics_metrics.description: PEERS are now created either by writ, or by patent: for those who claim by prescription must suppose either a writ or patent made to their ancestors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creation by writ is older but ennoblement occurs only when the person actually takes his seat; creation by patent is a royal grant and generally safer as it enures to grantee and heirs according to its limitations even if grantee never sits. Creation by writ holds to him and his heirs without words of limitation; letters patent require words directing inheritance or the dignity may be for life only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life peerages and limited inheritances
rubrics_metrics.description: A man or woman may be created noble for their own lives, and the dignity not descend to their heirs at all, or descend only to some particular heirs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters patent can limit descent (e.g., to a man and the heirs male of his body by Elizabeth his present lady), illustrating how patents can create non-descendible or specially limited peerages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of taking seat for creation by writ
rubrics_metrics.description: A man is not ennobled [by writ], unless he actually takes his seat in the house of lords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains practical distinction between writ and patent; cites Co. Litt.; notes practice of calling up eldest son by writ in father's barony to avoid loss if he never takes seat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial of peers by peers
rubrics_metrics.description: In criminal cases, a nobleman shall be tried by his peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: to avoid popular envy and secure privilege of being tried by equals (Magna Carta c.29). Notes possible exceptions (bishops may not be ennobled in blood and thus not peers for this purpose). Special statute (20 Hen. VI c.9) requires that peeresses (in their own right or by marriage) be tried before same judicature as peers. Rules on how marriage affects a woman's nobility and trial rights are explained (e.g., woman noble in her own right remains noble on marrying a commoner; noble by marriage may lose dignity by second marriage to commoner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege from civil arrest
rubrics_metrics.description: A peer, or peeress (either in her own right or by marriage) cannot be arrested in civil cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists other judicial peculiarities: a peer sitting in judgment gives verdict upon his honour (not oath); peers answer to bills in chancery upon honour; when examined as witnesses they must be sworn. Cites authorities (e.g., Salk., Cro. Car.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verdict and chancery answers 'upon honour' for peers
rubrics_metrics.description: A peer, sitting in judgment, gives not his verdict upon oath ... he answers also to bills in chancery upon his honour, and not upon his oath; but, when he is examined as a witness ... he must be sworn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes procedural treatment of peers in different judicial contexts and underscores the law's respect for peer honour while preserving general rules about witness oaths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scandalum magnatum (enhanced penalties for defaming peers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The honour of peers is ... much more penal to spread false reports of them ... called by the peculiar name of scandalum magnatum; and subjected to peculiar punishment by divers antient statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites statutes (3 Edw. I c.34; 2 Ric. II st.1 c.5; 12 Ric. II c.11) and explains that scandal against peers and certain high officers carries harsher penalties than ordinary defamation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of nobility only by death or attainder; degradation by parliament only
rubrics_metrics.description: A PEER cannot lose his nobility, but by death or attainder ... it is expressly held that a peer cannot be degraded but by act of parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes a singular historical instance (degradation of George Nevile by act of parliament in reign of Edward IV) but emphasizes modern authority that only an act of parliament can effect degradation; addresses prior opinions about royal power to degrade and rejects them by citation of later authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commoners as 'peers' in respect of lack of nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: The commonalty, like the nobility, are divided into several degrees; ... yet all are in law peers, in respect of their want of nobility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States the classification principle that commoners, despite internal gradations, are treated collectively as peers of the realm by virtue of not being noble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antient and modern orders of knighthood and precedence
rubrics_metrics.description: The first dignity after the nobility, is a knight of the order of St. George, or of the garter ... Next follows a knight banneret ... else he ranks after baronets ... Next follow knights of the bath ... The last of these inferior nobility are knights bachelors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains origins, creation methods, and relative precedence: knight banneret must be created by the king in person in the field under royal banners (in time of open war); baronetcy instituted 1611 by letters patent and descendible to male issue, with Ulster arms; knights of the bath derive name from ceremony of bathing. Historical notes on antiquity and decline of some forms of knighthood (e.g., knights as military tenures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Feudal military obligation (knight's fee: forty days service)
rubrics_metrics.description: By this means ... all the lands in the kingdom were divided into ... knight's fees ... and for every knight's fee a knight or soldier, miles, was bound to attend the king in his wars, for forty days in a year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains purpose (seasonal campaigns), the obligation to serve or pay a fine for non-compliance, and that commutation into pecuniary aids later occurred; notes abolition of military tenures at the Restoration (12 Car. II c.24).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and classes of esquires
rubrics_metrics.description: Esquires and gentlemen are confounded ... Camden distinguishes four sorts of esquires: 1. The eldest sons of knights, and their eldest sons, in perpetual succession. 2. The younger sons of peers, and their eldest sons. 3. Esquires created by the king's letters patent, or other investiture. 4. Esquires by virtue of their offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adds esquires of knights of the bath (three at installation), foreign and Irish peers, and the eldest sons of peers of Great Britain (who are esquires in law for legal proceedings). Cites Coke and Camden on distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of gentleman and yeoman
rubrics_metrics.description: A gentleman ... is one qui arma gerit, who bears coat armour ... A yeoman is he that hath free land of forty shillings by the year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains social criteria: gentleman associated with bearing arms, liberal education, idleness; yeoman qualified to serve on juries and vote for knights of the shire; statutory thresholds noted (40s freehold).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of style for tradesmen, artificers, and labourers in legal proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Tradesmen, artificers, and labourers ... must in pursuance of the statute 1 Hen. V. c. 5. be stiled by the name and addition of their estate, degree, or mystery, in all actions and other legal proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory requirement for how non-gentle classes must be described in pleadings and proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle against a distinct permanent military order in free states
rubrics_metrics.description: In a land of liberty it is extremely dangerous to make a distinct order of the profession of arms. ... In free states no man should take up arms, but with a view to defend his country and its laws: he puts not off the citizen when he enters the camp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that standing, professional military classes threaten liberty; references historical practices and continental examples; cites Montesquieu on need for armies to consist of the people to prevent executive oppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saxon military offices (dukes/heretochs) and election by people
rubrics_metrics.description: The military force ... was in the hands of the dukes or heretochs ... being taken out of the principal nobility ... Their duty was to lead and regulate the English armies ... they were elected by the people in their full assembly, or folkmote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes elective nature of these military leaders under Saxon constitution as check on power; historical examples of misuse (Edric duke of Mercia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of Winchester and obligation to provide arms; commissions of array
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute of Winchester obliged every man, according to his estate and degree, to provide a determinate quantity of such arms as were then in use, ... constables appointed in all hundreds to see that such arms were provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Later statutes altered weapons and provisions repealed under James I; while in force, commissions of array were issued and form settled in 5 Hen. IV; describes practical mustering and arraying of inhabitants for defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on compulsion to serve abroad without parliament
rubrics_metrics.description: It was provided, that no man should be compelled to go out of the kingdom at any rate, nor out of his shire but in cases of urgent necessity; nor should provide soldiers unless by consent of parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts legal limits on compelled foreign service and on raising soldiers without parliamentary consent; cites statutes (1 Edw III st.2 c.5 & 7; 25 Edw. III st.5 c.8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction and role of lord lieutenants
rubrics_metrics.description: About the reign of king Henry the eighth, and his children, lord lieutenants began to be introduced, as standing representatives of the crown, to keep the counties in military order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes early statutory mentions (4 & 5 Ph. & M. c.3) and that lieutenants were initially extraordinary magistrates in Elizabeth's time; later became regular county officers for militia organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Restoration militia organization and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The general scheme of which is to discipline a certain number of the inhabitants of every county, chosen by lot for three years, and officered by the lord lieutenant ... They are not compellable to march out of their counties, unless in case of invasion or actual rebellion, nor in any case compellable to march out of the kingdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Militia discipline generally liberal but subject to martial law when in actual service; statutes (13 Car. II c.6; 14 Car. II c.3; 15 Car. II c.4) underpin organization; modern acts reenact parts and add new regulations (30 Geo. II c.25 etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Martial law's limited legitimacy and prohibition in time of peace
rubrics_metrics.description: Martial law, which is built upon no settled principles, but is entirely arbitrary in its decisions, is ... in truth and reality no law ... it ought not to be permitted in time of peace, when the king's courts are open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives examples: reversal of attainder under martial law (Edm. earl of Kent) and statement that execution under colour of martial law in time of peace is murder. Cites Petition of Right (no soldier quartered without consent; no commission to proceed within land according to martial law) and Bill of Rights (raising/keeping standing army in peace without consent of parliament is against law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of standing armies and parliamentary control
rubrics_metrics.description: It has also for many years past been annually judged necessary by our legislature ... to maintain even in time of peace a standing body of troops ... who are however ipso facto disbanded at the expiration of every year, unless continued by parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains constitutional mechanism (annual renewal by parliament) limiting executive use of standing forces; historical rationale tied to national defense and balance of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutiny Act offences and court-martial punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: An annual act of parliament passes, 'to punish mutiny and desertion, and for the better payment of the army and their quarters.' ... if any officer and soldier shall excite, or join any mutiny ... or shall disobey his lawful commands; such offender shall suffer such punishment as a court martial shall inflict, though it extend to death itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists specific military offences (excite/join mutiny; failure to report; defection; sleeping on post; holding correspondence with enemy; violence toward superior; disobedience). Emphasizes potential for capital punishment at discretion of court martial guided by crown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crown's authority to make articles of war and constitute courts-martial
rubrics_metrics.description: 'His majesty ... may form articles of war, and constitute courts martial, with power to try any crime by such articles, and inflict such penalties as the articles direct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies substantial discretionary power vested in the crown regarding military offences and punishments; notes statutory limitation that certain punishments (life/limb) cannot be inflicted except for crimes declared by statute. Author suggests future statutory clarification of military subjection limits and express articles for army government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desertion: differential penalties in war and peace and current mutiny act practice
rubrics_metrics.description: By our standing laws desertion in time of war is made felony, without benefit of clergy ... yet, by our militia laws ... a much lighter punishment is inflicted for desertion in time of peace. But our mutiny act makes no such distinction: for any of the faults therein mentioned are, equally at all times, punishable with death itself, if a court martial shall think proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights inconsistency between older standing laws, militia statutes, and contemporary Mutiny Act; underscores the discretionary and severe potential punishments under courts-martial even in peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle that crimes and penalties ought to be ascertained; concern about soldier servitude
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the greatest advantages of our English law is, that not only the crimes themselves which it punishes, but also the penalties which it inflicts, are ascertained and notorious: nothing is left to arbitrary discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast drawn with military arbitrariness; cites Coke ('misera est servitus, ubi jus est vagum aut incognitum') and Montesquieu's caution that professional armies distinct from the people can threaten liberty. Recommends precautions: prevent introduction of slavery or don't entrust slaves/soldiers with arms; suggests mixing army and people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soldiers' statutory welfare and civil privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: By statute 43 Eliz. c. 3. a weekly allowance is to be raised in every county for the relief of soldiers that are sick, hurt, and maimed: not forgetting the royal hospital at Chelsea ... Officers and soldiers ... are by several statutes ... at liberty to use any trade or occupation ... notwithstanding any statute, custom, or charter to the contrary. And soldiers in actual military service may make their wills ... without those forms ... which the law requires in other cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerates statutory protections and benefits (weekly county allowances, Chelsea hospital, freedom to use trades/towns post-service, simplified testamentary formalities while in service) and cites relevant statutes (29 Car. II c.3; 5 W. III c.21 s.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maritime state as national defence and navigation laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The royal navy of England hath ever been its greatest defence and ornament ... To so much perfection was our naval reputation arrived in the twelfth century, that the code of maritime laws ... called the laws of Oleron ... was confessedly compiled by our king Richard the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes navy's centrality to national security; credits laws of Oleron and later Navigation Acts for promoting English shipping and seamen. Notes historical modesty of Elizabethan navy and later growth through statute.
